[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Buccleuch_Avon_%281885%29.png/250px-Buccleuch_Avon_%281885%29.png)](/wiki/File:Buccleuch_Avon_(1885).png)

[Buccleuch Avon](/wiki/Buccleuch_Avon "Buccleuch Avon"), whelped in 1885

The Labrador breed dates back to at least the 1830s, when [St John's water dogs](/wiki/St._John%27s_water_dog "St. John's water dog") bred by European settlers in [Newfoundland](/wiki/Newfoundland "Newfoundland") were first introduced to Britain from ships trading between Canada and [Poole](/wiki/Poole "Poole") in [Dorset](/wiki/Dorset "Dorset"). These were then bred with British hunting dogs to create what became known as the Labrador Retriever. Its early patrons included the [Earl of Malmesbury](/wiki/Earl_of_Malmesbury "Earl of Malmesbury"), the [Duke of Buccleuch](/wiki/Duke_of_Buccleuch "Duke of Buccleuch"), the [Earl of Home](/wiki/Earl_of_Home "Earl of Home") and [Sir John Scott](/wiki/Sir_John_Scott "Sir John Scott"). Early writers have confused the Labrador with the much larger [Newfoundland](/wiki/Newfoundland_(dog) "Newfoundland (dog)") and the [Lesser Newfoundland](/wiki/Lesser_Newfoundland "Lesser Newfoundland"), with [Charles William George St John](/wiki/Charles_William_George_St_John "Charles William George St John") even referring to the Lesser Newfoundland as the Newfoundland. Colonel [Peter Hawker](/wiki/Peter_Hawker "Peter Hawker") describes the first Labrador as being not larger than an [English Pointer](/wiki/Pointer_(dog_breed) "Pointer (dog breed)"), more often black than other colours, long in its head and nose with a deep chest, fine legs, and short and smooth coat, and did not carry its tail as highly as the Newfoundland.[[5]](#cite_note-Drury1903-5) Hawker distinguishes the Newfoundland from both the "proper Labrador" and St John's breed of these dogs[[5]](#cite_note-Drury1903-5)[[6]](#cite_note-Hawker1846-6) in the fifth edition of his book *Instructions to You

L'Oréal purchased Synthélabo, a pharmaceutical company, in 1973. Synthélabo merged with [Sanofi](/wiki/Sanofi "Sanofi") in 1999 to become [Sanofi-Synthélabo](/wiki/Sanofi-Synth%C3%A9labo "Sanofi-Synthélabo"). Sanofi-Synthélabo merged with [Aventis](/wiki/Aventis "Aventis") in 2004 to become [Sanofi-Aventis](/wiki/Sanofi-Aventis "Sanofi-Aventis").[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Nestlé has owned a stake in L'Oréal since 1974, when it bought into the company at the request of [Liliane Bettencourt](/wiki/Liliane_Bettencourt "Liliane Bettencourt"), the daughter of the founder of L'Oréal.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

In 1984, L'Oréal acquired part of [Helena Rubinstein Incorporated](/wiki/Helena_Rubinstein_Incorporated "Helena Rubinstein Incorporated") from Albi International. The portions acquired were the Japanese and Latin American divisions of the company, along with overseeing the operations and the markets for those divisions.[[14]](#cite_note-WEILJ-14) The joint venture partnership between L'Oréal and Albi International lasted until 1988, when L'Oréal brought the remainder of the company and has owned the entire company since then.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

From 1988 to 1989, L'Oréal controlled the film company [Paravision International](/wiki/Paravision_International "Paravision International"), whose properties included the [Filmation](/wiki/Filmation "Filmation") and [De Laurentiis](/wiki/De_Laurentiis_Entertainment_Group "De Laurentiis Entertainment Group") libraries. [StudioCanal](/wiki/StudioCanal "StudioCanal") acquired the Paravision properties in 1994.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

On 17 March 2006, L'Oréal purchased cosmetics company [The Body Shop](/wiki/The_Body_Shop "The Body Shop") for £562 million.[[17]](#cite_note-17) In May 2008, L'Oréal acquired YSL Beauté for $1.8 billion.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

fanoutqa_013987.x:
List of largest cities :: Definitions :: Urban area :: chunk_0003
Main article: [Urban area](/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area")

A city can be defined as a conditionally [contiguous](/wiki/Geographic_contiguity "Geographic contiguity") [urban area](/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area"), with relatively less regard to territorial or administrative boundaries. [UNICEF](/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF") defines urban area as follows:

> The definition of "urban" varies from country to country, and, with periodic reclassification, can also vary within one country over time, making direct comparisons difficult. An urban area can be defined by one or more of the following: administrative criteria or political boundaries (e.g., area within the jurisdiction of a municipality or town committee), a threshold population size (where the minimum for an urban settlement is typically in the region of 2,000 people, although this varies globally between 200 and 50,000), population density, economic function (e.g., where a significant majority of the population is not primarily engaged in agriculture, or where there is surplus employment) or the presence of urban characteristics (e.g., paved streets, electric lighting, sewerage).

According to [Demographia](/wiki/Demographia "Demographia"), an urban area is a continuously built up land mass of urban development that is within a labor market (metropolitan area or metropolitan region) and contains no [rural land](/wiki/Rural_area "Rural area").

For more variety of estimates, see [Megacity § List of megacities](/wiki/Megacity#List_of_megacities "Megacity").

There are 83 cities in the world with a population exceeding 5 million people, according to 2025 estimates by the [United Nations](/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations").[[11]](#cite_note-UNpopulation-11)

Main article: [Gerald Ford Supreme Court candidates](/wiki/Gerald_Ford_Supreme_Court_candidates "Gerald Ford Supreme Court candidates")

In 1975, Ford appointed [John Paul Stevens](/wiki/John_Paul_Stevens "John Paul Stevens") as [Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States](/wiki/Associate_Justice_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States") to replace retiring Justice [William O. Douglas](/wiki/William_O._Douglas "William O. Douglas"). Stevens had been a judge of the [United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit](/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Seventh_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit"), appointed by President Nixon.[[155]](#cite_note-stephensJP-155) During his tenure as House Republican leader, Ford had led efforts to have Douglas impeached.[[156]](#cite_note-156) After being confirmed, Stevens eventually disappointed some conservatives by siding with the Court's liberal wing regarding the outcome of many key issues.[[157]](#cite_note-persuasion-157) Nevertheless, in 2005 Ford praised Stevens. "He has served his nation well," Ford said of Stevens, "with dignity, intellect and without partisan political concerns."[[158]](#cite_note-158)

Main article: [List of federal judges appointed by Gerald Ford](/wiki/List_of_federal_judges_appointed_by_Gerald_Ford "List of federal judges appointed by Gerald Ford")

Ford appointed 11 judges to the United States Courts of Appeals, and 50 judges to the [United States district courts](/wiki/United_States_district_court "United States district court").[[159]](#cite_note-159)

Barra started working for General Motors in 1980 as a [co-op student](/wiki/Cooperative_education "Cooperative education") when she was 18 years old.[[12]](#cite_note-shm-12) Her job was checking fender panels and inspecting hoods, and she used this job to pay for her college tuition.[[13]](#cite_note-13) She subsequently held a variety of engineering and administrative positions, including managing the [Detroit/Hamtramck Assembly](/wiki/Detroit/Hamtramck_Assembly "Detroit/Hamtramck Assembly") plant.[[11]](#cite_note-bb-11)

In February 2008, she became vice president of Global Manufacturing Engineering. In July 2009, she advanced to the position of vice president of Global Human Resources, which she held until February 2011 when she was named executive vice president of Global Product Development.[[11]](#cite_note-bb-11)[[14]](#cite_note-14) The latter position included responsibilities for design; she worked to reduce the number of [automobile platforms](/wiki/Automobile_platforms "Automobile platforms") in [GM](/wiki/List_of_GM_platforms "List of GM platforms").[[3]](#cite_note-nyt-3) In August 2013, her vice president responsibility was extended to include Global Purchasing and Supply Chain.[[15]](#cite_note-gm-15)

When Barra took over as chief executive of General Motors in January 2014, she became the first female head of an automobile manufacturer.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

By the fourth quarter of 1985, *USA Today* had become the second-largest newspaper in the United States, reaching a daily circulation of 1.4 million copies. Total daily readership of the paper by 1987 (according to Simmons Market Research Bureau statistics) had reached 5.5 million, the largest of any daily newspaper in the U.S. On May 6, 1986, *USA Today* began production of its international edition in [Switzerland](/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"). *USA Today* operated at a loss for most of its first four years of operation, accumulating a total deficit of $233 million after taxes. According to figures released by Gannett in July 1987, the newspaper began turning its first profit in May 1987, six months ahead of Gannett's corporate revenue projections.[[12]](#cite_note-timeline-12)

On January 29, 1988, *USA Today* published the largest edition in its history, a 78-page weekend edition featuring a section previewing [Super Bowl XXII](/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXII "Super Bowl XXII"); the edition included 44.38 pages of advertising and sold 2,114,055 copies, setting a single-day record for an American newspaper (and surpassed seven months later on September 2, when its [Labor Day](/wiki/Labor_Day "Labor Day") weekend edition sold 2,257,734 copies). On April 15, *USA Today* launched a third international printing site, based in [Hong Kong](/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong"). The international edition set circulation and advertising records during August 1988, with coverage of the [1988 Summer Olympics](/wiki/1988_Summer_Olympics "1988 Summer Olympics"), selling more than 60,000 copies and 100 pages of advertising.[[12]](#cite_note-timeline-12)

The site's critical consensus states "*Only Yesterday*'s long-delayed U.S. debut fills a frustrating gap for American Ghibli fans while offering further proof of the studio's incredibly consistent commitment to quality."[[60]](#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes-61) On [Metacritic](/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") the film has a weighted average score of 90 out of 100 based on 19 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".[[61]](#cite_note-Metacritic-62)

[Roger Ebert](/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") gave the film a very favorable review in his essay regarding anime and the other work of Studio Ghibli calling it "a touching, melancholy meditation on the life of the same woman at ages 10 and 27."[[62]](#cite_note-Ebert_1999-63) Nicolas Rapold, of *[The New York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, gave the film a positive review, saying, "Mr. Takahata's psychologically acute film, which was based on a manga, seems to grow in impact, too, as the adult Taeko comes to a richer understanding of what she wants and how she wants to live."[[63]](#cite_note-Repold_2016-64) [Glenn Kenny](/wiki/Glenn_Kenny "Glenn Kenny") of [RogerEbert.com](/wiki/RogerEbert.com "RogerEbert.com") awarded it a similarly positive review, saying "Like *[Kaguya](/wiki/The_Tale_of_the_Princess_Kaguya_(film) "The Tale of the Princess Kaguya (film)")*, it functions as a highly sensitive and empathetic consideration of the situation of women in Japanese society—but it's also a breathtaking work of art on its own."[[64]](#cite_note-Kenny_2015-65)

**Nigeria**,[[b]](#cite_note-12) officially the **Federal Republic of Nigeria**, is a country in [West Africa](/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa") between the [Sahel](/wiki/Sahel "Sahel") to the north and the [Gulf of Guinea](/wiki/Gulf_of_Guinea "Gulf of Guinea") in the [Atlantic Ocean](/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") to the south. It covers an area of 923,769 square kilometres (356,669 mi2). With [a population](/wiki/Demographics_of_Nigeria "Demographics of Nigeria") of more than 242 million, it is the [most populous country](/wiki/List_of_African_countries_by_population "List of African countries by population") in [Africa](/wiki/Africa "Africa"), and the [world's sixth-most populous country](/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population "List of countries and dependencies by population"). Nigeria borders [Niger](/wiki/Niger "Niger") in [the north](/wiki/Niger%E2%80%93Nigeria_border "Niger–Nigeria border"), [Chad](/wiki/Chad "Chad") in [the northeast](/wiki/Chad%E2%80%93Nigeria_border "Chad–Nigeria border"), [Cameroon](/wiki/Cameroon "Cameroon") in [the east](/wiki/Cameroon%E2%80%93Nigeria_border "Cameroon–Nigeria border"), and [Benin](/wiki/Benin "Benin") in [the west](/wiki/Benin%E2%80%93Nigeria_border "Benin–Nigeria border"). Nigeria is a [federal republic](/wiki/Federation "Federation") comprising 36 [states](/wiki/States_of_Nigeria "States of Nigeria") and the [Federal Capital Territory](/wiki/Federal_Capital_Territory,_Nigeria "Federal Capital Territory, Nigeria"), where its capital, [Abuja](/wiki/Abuja "Abuja"), is located. The [largest city in Nigeria](/wiki/List_of_Nigerian_cities_by_population "List of Nigerian cities by population") by population is [Lagos](/wiki/Lagos "Lagos"), one of the largest [metropolitan areas](/wiki/List_of_largest_cities "List of largest cities") in the world and the [largest in Africa](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Africa_by_population "List of cities in Africa by population").
